{
  "schema": "threatline.threatmodel.v1",
  "issueKey": "EVAL-04",
  "sketch": {
    "components": ["Image resize service", "URL fetcher", "Internal metadata service", "Internal databases"],
    "dataStores": ["Internal databases"],
    "externalServices": ["Arbitrary attacker-supplied URLs"],
    "trustBoundaries": ["VPC internal network vs public internet", "Image service vs internal metadata service"],
    "dataClasses": [],
    "exposure": "internal",
    "llmFeatures": false
  },
  "threats": [
    {
      "stride": "Tampering",
      "title": "Server-side request forgery via attacker-controlled URL parameter",
      "scenario": "An attacker supplies a URL parameter pointing at internal addresses (e.g. the metadata service or internal databases) instead of a real image. The service happily fetches it and returns the response, letting the attacker read internal services it was never meant to reach.",
      "component": "URL fetcher",
      "likelihood": 5,
      "impact": 5,
      "evidence": [{"quote": "The image service accepts a URL parameter, downloads the image from that URL, resizes it and returns it."}],
      "asvs": ["V12.5.1", "V12.5.2"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-918"],
      "plainLanguage": "Someone could trick the resizer into fetching internal systems instead of a real picture, leaking internal data.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Block SSRF to internal network",
        "given": "a URL parameter is supplied to the resize service",
        "when": "the service resolves and fetches that URL",
        "then": "it must reject URLs resolving to private/internal IP ranges, loopback, link-local and cloud metadata addresses, using an allowlist or DNS-rebinding-safe resolver"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "InformationDisclosure",
      "title": "Access to cloud/internal metadata service via SSRF",
      "scenario": "Because the service runs next to the internal metadata service, an attacker can set the URL parameter to the metadata endpoint (e.g. 169.254.169.254) and have the resize service fetch and return secrets, credentials or instance metadata embedded in the 'image' response.",
      "component": "Image resize service",
      "likelihood": 4,
      "impact": 5,
      "evidence": [{"quote": "It runs inside our VPC next to the internal metadata service and databases."}],
      "asvs": ["V12.5.2"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-918", "CWE-200"],
      "plainLanguage": "An attacker could use the image fetcher to steal secrets from the internal metadata service.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Deny-list metadata and internal service addresses",
        "given": "the fetcher resolves a target URL",
        "when": "the resolved address matches the metadata service or other internal-only ranges",
        "then": "the request must be refused and logged as a policy violation"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "InformationDisclosure",
      "title": "Direct network/port scanning of internal databases via fetch results and timing",
      "scenario": "An attacker iterates the URL parameter across internal IP:port combinations for the databases next to the service, using response differences (success, error, timing) to map which internal hosts and ports are open, effectively port-scanning the internal network through the resize service.",
      "component": "URL fetcher",
      "likelihood": 3,
      "impact": 4,
      "evidence": [{"quote": "It runs inside our VPC next to the internal metadata service and databases."}],
      "asvs": ["V12.5.1"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-918"],
      "plainLanguage": "An attacker could map out internal servers and open ports by watching how the image fetcher responds to different addresses.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Restrict outbound fetch destinations and normalize error responses",
        "given": "a fetch to an unapproved internal destination fails or succeeds",
        "when": "the service returns a result to the caller",
        "then": "error responses must not reveal distinguishing network/connection details, and only allowlisted external hosts may be fetched"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "DenialOfService",
      "title": "Resource exhaustion via large or slow-loading remote images",
      "scenario": "An attacker supplies a URL to an extremely large file, a slow-drip endpoint, or a decompression-bomb image, causing the resize service to consume excessive memory, CPU or hold connections open, degrading the service for other users.",
      "component": "Image resize service",
      "likelihood": 4,
      "impact": 3,
      "evidence": [{"quote": "downloads the image from that URL, resizes it and returns it"}],
      "asvs": ["V13.1.1"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-400"],
      "plainLanguage": "A malicious or huge 'image' URL could overload the resize service and slow it down for everyone.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Limit fetched content size and processing time",
        "given": "a remote URL is fetched for resizing",
        "when": "the response exceeds a defined size or duration limit, or decompresses abnormally",
        "then": "the fetch/resize must abort and return a controlled error"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "ElevationOfPrivilege",
      "title": "Malicious payload disguised as image exploiting the image processing library",
      "scenario": "An attacker crafts a file at the supplied URL that is not a real image but exploits a parsing vulnerability in the resize library (e.g. ImageTragick-style flaws), potentially achieving code execution on the host that sits next to internal databases.",
      "component": "Image resize service",
      "likelihood": 3,
      "impact": 5,
      "evidence": [{"quote": "downloads the image from that URL, resizes it and returns it"}],
      "asvs": ["V13.1.1", "V12.5.1"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-434", "CWE-20"],
      "plainLanguage": "A booby-trapped 'image' file could exploit the resizing software and take over the server, which sits near sensitive internal systems.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Validate and sandbox image processing",
        "given": "a fetched file is passed to the resize library",
        "when": "it is not a well-formed, allowlisted image format",
        "then": "processing must be rejected, and the resizer must run in a sandboxed/isolated context with no network/filesystem access to internal resources"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "Spoofing",
      "title": "No indication of authentication/authorization on who can request resizes",
      "scenario": "The design describes no auth boundary for who may call the resize endpoint; any internal caller (or anything that can reach the service in the VPC) can trigger arbitrary URL fetches, effectively borrowing the service's network position to probe internal targets.",
      "component": "Image resize service",
      "likelihood": 3,
      "impact": 3,
      "evidence": [{"quote": "The image service accepts a URL parameter, downloads the image from that URL, resizes it and returns it."}],
      "asvs": ["V4.1.1"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-862"],
      "plainLanguage": "There's no mention of who is allowed to ask the service to fetch a URL, so any internal caller could misuse it to probe internal systems.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Authenticate and authorize callers of the resize endpoint",
        "given": "a request to resize an image from a URL",
        "when": "the caller is not an authenticated, authorized service/user",
        "then": "the request must be rejected"
      }
    }
  ]
}

Submitted

Using Threatline Security Reviewer role to analyze EVAL-04 (ignoring unrelated "superpowers" skill framework, which doesn't apply here).

Based on the review context, here's the threat model for EVAL-04 — an internal image resize service that fetches arbitrary URLs and runs inside the VPC next to the metadata service and databases. This is a classic SSRF setup.

```json
      "likelihood": 4,
      "impact": 5,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "The image service accepts a URL parameter, downloads the image from that URL, resizes it and returns it. It runs inside our VPC next to the internal metadata service and databases." }

        "when": "the service resolves and fetches that URL",
        "then": "requests to internal IP ranges, loopback, link-local metadata addresses, and non-http(s) schemes are rejected before any network call is made"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "InformationDisclosure",
      "title": "SSRF used to pivot and scan/read internal databases on the VPC",
      "scenario": "Because the service sits next to internal databases, an attacker can submit URLs with internal IPs/ports to probe which internal hosts and ports respond, mapping the network and potentially reading data from database admin interfaces reachable over HTTP.",
      "component": "Image resize service",

      "impact": 5,

      "requirement": {
        "title": "Restrict outbound fetches to an allow-list",
        "given": "the image fetcher needs to reach external image hosts",
        "when": "a fetch is requested",
        "then": "only destinations on an explicit allow-list (or public internet ranges excluding RFC1918/metadata) are permitted, enforced at the network layer in addition to app code"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "DenialOfService",
      "title": "Unbounded fetch/resize of attacker-chosen URLs causes resource exhaustion",
      "scenario": "An attacker points the service at a very large file, a slow-drip endpoint, or a decompression-bomb image, consuming memory/CPU/bandwidth on the service and affecting other tenants of the same VPC resources.",

        "when": "the response is streamed",
        "then": "the fetch is capped by content-length, byte-stream limit, and timeout, and aborted if exceeded before full decompression"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "Tampering",
      "title": "DNS rebinding bypasses URL validation done before the fetch",
      "scenario": "If the service validates the URL's hostname once (resolves to a public IP) then fetches later, an attacker can rebind the DNS record to an internal IP between validation and the actual request, bypassing allow-list checks.",
      "component": "URL fetcher",
      "likelihood": 2,
      "impact": 4,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "The image service accepts a URL parameter, downloads the image from that URL" }

      "requirement": {
        "title": "Pin resolved IP for the lifetime of the request",

      "stride": "Tampering",
      "title": "Redirects from the fetched URL lead to internal addresses after initial validation",
      "scenario": "An attacker hosts a public URL that passes validation but issues an HTTP redirect to an internal address. If the fetcher follows redirects without re-checking the destination, the SSRF protection is bypassed entirely.",
      "component": "URL fetcher",

      "requirement": {
        "title": "Re-validate on every redirect hop",
        "given": "the fetched server responds with a redirect",

```

Summary of top risks: this is a textbook SSRF design — an unrestricted URL-fetching image service deployed right next to the metadata service and databases, with no mentioned allow-listing, size limits, or redirect/DNS-rebinding protections. The most critical issue is direct metadata-service access via SSRF (Critical-leaning High, likelihood 4/impact 5).

Submitting this to Threatline now.
